summary: A steel lighthouse on a stone-filled crib in the Manitou Passage, built in 1935 to replace a lightship, staffed until 1980 and now restored by a nonprofit.

access.note: Privately owned by North Manitou Light Keepers; offshore, boat only; ticketed guided tours from Leland Harbor.

evidence.supports: lightship from White Shoal 1910; three lightships
evidence.quote: When White Shoal Lighthouse was finished in 1910, the lightship formerly used there was transferred to North Manitou Shoal. Three lightships served on the station: LV-56 from 1910 to 1926, LV-89 from 1927 to 1933, and LV-103/WAL-526 from 1934 to 1935.

As the lightship was often compelled by ice conditions to be off its station in the early spring and late fall, in 1923 the Lighthouse Service proposed replacing the lightship by a fixed station on a crib that would allow the fog signal on North Manitou Island to be discontinued

Funds for construction of North Manitou Shoal Lighthouse were provided by the Public Works Administration, and construction started early in the fall of 1933.
The crib on which the structure is built stands in 22 feet of water, on a hard sand and coarse stone bottom. The crib is 65 feet square by 22 feet deep, and is filled with conveyor stone.
Arch web steel sheet piling driven 24 feet into lake bottom encloses and protects the crib.
The crib supports a hollow pier of reinforced concrete 62 feet square and 20 feet above water, with deck overhanging 2 feet on all sides.
This hollow space is occupied by the steam heating plant, coal and oil storage, laundry, etc.
Above the pier rises the steel building 37 feet square, two stories high, surmounted by a square tower of three stories additional height.
On the top of the tower is a third-order lantern, with its focal plane 79 feet above water.
The illuminating apparatus is a four-panel, 36-inch diameter revolving lens, fitted with a 1,000-watt electric lamp producing a flashing red light of 240,000 candlepower.
Current is supplied from 4-kilowatt Diesel engine-generators with storage batteries.
Two diaphragm horns, one facing up and one facing down the channel, sound, simultaneously
The radiobeacon is synchronized with the sound signal for distance-finding purposes.
This light station replaces the North Manitou Lightship No. 103 and North Manitou Island Light Station
In the second story is a large living and watch room, one end of which is occupied by kitchen equipment.
Four bedrooms are also located on the second floor.
The station was constructed at a total cost of $152,186.

In May 2015, North Manitou Shoal Lighthouse was declared excess to the needs of the United States Coast Guard and made available to eligible organizations under the provisions of the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act of 2000.

notes_for_editor: NRHP nomination PDF is not digitised, so no nomination-based chronology. No newspaper hits for 1933-1940. LighthouseFriends is the only source for construction history, auction and restoration; its text quotes the Lighthouse Service's 1935 description, whose original I did not see. Disagreements flagged in text: optic (third-order lantern with 4-panel lens per LF vs fourth-order per USLHS) and Machulis dates (USLHS at least 1958; LF ending 1958). Glenn Furst's remembered fog quote concerns the earlier North Manitou Island light, and is used as predecessor context. Keeper roster comes from USLHS archive only; confirm in primary records. Coast Guard crew roster (about 40 names, 1960-1971) was not copied into the keepers array, so add if the roster table should show them.
